full_judgment:
34. It is a fundamental principle of criminal trial that the accused is presumed to be innocent and therefore the burden lays on the prosecution to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt. The prosecution in the present case is therefore required to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the condemned prisoner caused the death of the aforesaid 2 persons of his family with the requisite intention namely, the mens rea as described under section 299 of the Penal Code. This general burden never shifts and it always rests on the prosecution. But the raising of the defence plea of insanity is envisaged under section 84 of the Penal Code that the accused by reason of his unsoundness of mind was incapable of knowing the nature of his act or what he was doing was either wrong or contrary to law. This being an exception, under section 105 of the Evidence Act, the burden of proving the existence of circumstances bringing the case within the said exception lies on the accused. Because in law until the contrary is proved, every man is presumed to be sane and possessed of a sufficient degree of reason to be responsible for his actions. In other words, the condemned prisoner has to rebut the presumption that such circumstance did not exist by placing materials before the Court sufficient to make it consider the existence of the said circumstance so probable that a prudent man would act on them. The condemned prisoner is, therefore, required to satisfy the standard of a prudent man. 

 35. Every man is presumed to be sane. This presumption does not apply to a man whose case is governed by section 84 of the Penal Code. Section 84 mentions the legal test of responsibility in case of alleged unsoundness of mind. It is by this test, as distinguished from medical test, that the criminality of the act is to be determined. This section in substance is the same as the McNaghtan Rules followed in the English jurisdiction. These Rules are still regarded as authoritative statement of the law as to criminal responsibility. 

 36. If the materials available on record in the present case, such as oral and documentary evidence, presumptions or even the prosecution evidence satisfy the test of a "prudent man" the condemned prisoner will be taken to have discharged his burden. But if the evidence so available on record in the case is not sufficient to discharge the burden under section 105 of the Evidence Act, but if it raises a reasonable doubt in the mind of the Court as regards any or more of the necessary ingredients of the offence charged creating a reasonable doubt in the mind of the court as to whether the condemned prisoner had the requisite mens rea as laid down in section 299 of the Penal Code, the condemned prisoner will be entitled to an acquittal in this case. Because in that even the prosecution will be taken to have failed to prove conclusively the guilt of the condemned prisoner.
